summary: Discusses deployment issues and requirements for operating Dual-Stack Lite, covering the deployment considerations and applicability of the DS-Lite architecture. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Dual-Stack Lite lets a provider offer IPv4 service over an IPv6-only network by tunnelling IPv4 packets and sharing one public IPv4 address between many users. This RFC lists the practical problems that causes and the settings operators should choose, such as how to log traffic and how to survive a router failure. It is a deployment guide, not a protocol specification.

subtitle: What to watch out for when running Dual-Stack Lite: tunnel overhead, logging, accounting and failover.

tldr.problem: An operator moving to IPv6 still has to offer IPv4 service, and sharing one public IPv4 address between many subscribers creates deployment problems that no single specification covers.
tldr.mechanism: The document collects guidance for running Dual-Stack Lite: where to place the AFTR, how much tunnel overhead to allow, what to log, where to do accounting, and how to keep the service available when an AFTR fails.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that adds no protocol of its own. The guidance comes from real deployment experience and covers the areas where operators are most likely to go wrong.

today: RFC 6908 is an Informational RFC published in March 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it stands as a catalogue of deployment guidance for Dual-Stack Lite rather than as a protocol specification.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
DS-Lite (RFC 6333) is a transition technique that lets an operator share public IPv4 addresses while provisioning only IPv6 to users. It is designed to keep offering IPv4 services while the network is upgraded to IPv6 step by step. DS-Lite combines an IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire (RFC 2473) with a Network Address Translator IPv4/IPv4, NAT44 (RFC 3022), so that more than one user can share a single public IPv4 address.

This document does not define a new protocol. Appendix A of RFC 6333 already explains how to deploy DS-Lite in specific scenarios. The purpose here is to describe the problems that arise during deployment and the guidance that mitigates them. The information is based on real deployment experience, compiled into one document so that operators do not have to search through several RFCs to work out which sections apply to them.

Two elements carry the design. The Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) sits inside the operator's network and is where the tunnel ends. The Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) element sits in the customer's home gateway or host and starts the tunnel. The document then works through AFTR considerations, B4 considerations, and the security questions that follow from the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Dual-Stack Lite carries IPv4 traffic across an IPv6-only network inside a tunnel, and shares one public IPv4 address between many users. This RFC lists the practical problems that creates and how operators should handle them.

sections.title: The AFTR and the B4
sections.content:
The AFTR is deployed inside the operator's network, as a stand-alone device or embedded in a router. It is the point where the IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel ends and where NAT44 is applied. It sits at the border between the IPv4 and the IPv6 networks: the tunnel interface on the AFTR is IPv6 and the external NAT44 interface is IPv4.

The B4 is a function on a dual-stack-capable node, either a host device or a home gateway. It creates the tunnel to the AFTR. An operator can configure the tunnel termination and the NAT44 function on a single physical interface, keeping them logically separated, but the RFC recommends two separate interfaces so that the two functions are segregated. In the common deployment the access network between the B4 and the AFTR is IPv6-only and the network between the AFTR and the IPv4 network is IPv4-only, and those two networks should reach the AFTR through two physical interfaces.

Where the AFTR sits changes the traffic pattern. In Model One the AFTR is at the edge of the network and covers a small region: it serves fewer B4s, needs less capacity and spreads traffic more evenly, but more AFTRs are needed and the operating cost rises with the amount of equipment. In Model Two the AFTR is at the core and covers a large region, so a few more powerful AFTRs can serve the whole user base. The RFC notes that DS-Lite can be deployed incrementally: an operator can start with Model Two and push the AFTRs towards the edge as demand grows, which turns the deployment into Model One.

Centralising the public IPv4 address also removes a signal that remote services used to rely on. Because an IPv4 address and IPv4 routing information no longer reveal where a host is, an application that locates hosts by their IPv4 address can put a subscriber in the wrong city. The RFC's mitigation is to deploy the AFTR as close to the B4s as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The AFTR is the provider's tunnel endpoint and does the address translation. The B4 is the piece in the customer's home gateway that starts the tunnel. The RFC recommends separate interfaces for the two jobs, and placing the AFTR near the subscribers.

sections.title: MTU and Fragmentation
sections.content:
DS-Lite is a tunnelling protocol, and tunnelling adds overhead to every packet, which lowers the effective MTU after encapsulation. Users can hit this as an inability to download web pages or to transfer large files.

The RFC says fragmentation and reassembly are not optimal, so the operator should do everything possible to eliminate the need for them. With a plain IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire, the MTU size of the IPv6 network between the B4 and the AFTR should account for the additional 40 bytes of overhead. If the access network MTU size is fixed and cannot be changed, the operator has to be aware that the B4 and the AFTR must support fragmentation as defined in RFC 6333.

Reassembly at the tunnel exit point is resource intensive, because a large number of B4s may terminate on the same AFTR. Where fragmentation cannot be avoided, the RFC advises scaling the AFTR for that scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping IPv4 inside IPv6 makes packets bigger, so less room is left for data. The RFC says to size the IPv6 network for 40 bytes of extra overhead and to avoid fragmenting packets if at all possible.

sections.title: Logging and Shared IPv4 Addresses
sections.content:
A source-specific log is essential for backtracking a specific host when a problem is identified with one of the AFTR's NAT-ed addresses. The log holds the B4's IPv6 source address, the transport protocol, the source port and the source IPv4 address after it has been NAT-ed. With that combination an operator can identify one host uniquely when a DS-Lite subscriber has trouble reaching the IPv4 network.

To maximise the IPv4 sharing ratio an operator may configure a short timeout for the NAT44 entries, which results in a large number of log records. Operators who want to aggregate the logs can configure the AFTR to preallocate a range of ports to each B4. That range is used in the NAT44 function, and the AFTR writes one log entry for the whole range, which can significantly reduce the log size.

Some operators need destination information as well, which the RFC calls a destination-specific log. It holds the B4's IPv6 address, transport protocol, source port, source IPv4 address after NAT, destination port and destination IPv4 address. This log is session based, so entries cannot be aggregated, and some AFTR implementations keep the logs in main memory, which is intensive in CPU and memory. The RFC advises configuring the AFTR to send logs periodically to a storage facility and then purge them from the AFTR.

Because many B4s share one public IPv4 address, a blacklisting decision by a remote peer can affect several users at once. Internet hosts may not be aware that a given single IPv4 address is actually shared, so a content provider that blocks one address stops the service for every B4 sharing it. The operator then receives calls about the outage and has to take corrective action.
sections.plainLanguage: Each NAT-ed subscriber needs a log saying which home gateway sent the traffic. The RFC explains how to keep those logs small, and warns that blocking a shared public address can cut off several subscribers at once.

sections.title: Policies, Accounting and Reliability
sections.content:
The AFTR applies two kinds of policy. Outgoing policies apply to packets originating from the B4s and should be provisioned on the AFTR's IPv6 interface. Incoming policies apply to packets originating from IPv4 networks and should be provisioned on the IPv4 interface. Outgoing policies may include access control list and quality of service settings: an operator can accept only connections that originated from specific IPv6 prefixes, give priority to packets marked with certain Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) values, or limit the rate of port allocation for a single B4's IPv6 address. Incoming packets are normally treated equally, so incoming policies are applied globally, for example marking every incoming packet with a predefined DSCP value.

Accounting for IPv4 traffic needs care. Because IPv4 traffic is encapsulated in IPv6 packets at the B4 and only decapsulated at the AFTR, the edge router needs additional functionality to associate IPv4 accounting information with the B4's IPv6 address. If DS-Lite is the only application using IPv4-in-IPv6 in the access network, the edge router can check the IPv6 Next Header field, identify the protocol type as 0x04, and collect the IPv4 accounting information. The AFTR may perform that accounting instead, but in a DSL deployment the AAA transaction happens between the edge router and the AAA server, and RFC 6333 does not require the AFTR to interact with either, so the AFTR may not hold the AAA parameters it needs to generate a complete IPv4 accounting record. IPv4 traffic accounting at the AFTR is therefore not recommended in that case. The RFC also notes that the data the edge router collects for IPv6 traffic already contains the total amount of traffic, because the IPv4 traffic is inside the IPv6 packets.

Reliability comes from running more than one AFTR, with the same IPv6 prefixes and the same tunnelling algorithm configured on each. DS-Lite is a stateful mechanism, so all the requirements for load balancing and failover apply. Two modes are described. In Cold Standby mode the states are not replicated from the primary to the backup, so when the primary fails all the existing established sessions are flushed out and the internal hosts must re-establish them with the external hosts. In Hot Standby mode the session states are replicated on the fly, so the backup takes over the established sessions and the internal hosts do not have to re-establish them. The RFC recommends Cold Standby for most deployment scenarios, because it needs no state synchronisation and any AFTR with extra capacity can take over.

Two further points concern services behind the B4. Applications that need to accept incoming connections require port forwarding managed in the serving AFTR, and the RFC suggests deploying the Port Control Protocol server there, with a PCP client in the B4s. Because a shared IPv4 address does not make every port available to every B4, the restricted ports 0 to 1023, which include well known TCP ports such as 25 and 80, should not be allocated to regular DS-Lite B4s, so that provisioning stays uniform. Separately, the B4 needs the IPv6 address of the AFTR, which can be configured out of band, by hand, through a DHCPv6 option or through RADIUS, and the B4 should send DNS queries to an external recursive resolver over IPv6 through a proxy resolver that follows RFC 5625.
sections.plainLanguage: The AFTR applies separate policies to traffic arriving from subscribers and traffic arriving from the IPv4 side. The RFC also covers where to count IPv4 traffic, how to fail over to a second AFTR, and how to forward ports for applications behind a subscriber's gateway.

sections.title: Tunnel Security and Document Security
sections.content:
RFC 6333, Section 11 describes the security issues of the DS-Lite mechanism itself. For the tunnel, the RFC gives the operator a way to restrict the service to registered B4s: implement the Outgoing Policy on the AFTR's tunnel interface so that it accepts only the IPv6 prefixes defined in that policy. Static provisioning means knowing in advance which IPv6 prefixes have been given to the B4s for the softwire. To simplify operation, AFTRs in the same region should be configured with the same Outgoing Policy for IPv6 prefixes, so that they accept both the regular connections and the failover connections from the B4s in that region.

The document's own Security Considerations section is short. It says the document presents no new security issues and that RFC 6333 discusses the DS-Lite related security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The AFTR can be set to accept tunnel traffic only from the IPv6 prefixes that were handed out to subscribers. The RFC adds no security analysis of its own and points to the Dual-Stack Lite specification for that.
